title: Robotx Solutions Inc. (May 2017 TCC) Tax Court Ruling
subject: Robotics company SR&ED appeal assessing whether automated system design and integration qualified for tax credits.
summary: Robotx Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 73, is a Tax Court of Canada decision applying the subsection 248(1) Income Tax Act definition of SR&ED to custom client engineering contracts. The Court upheld the denial of $182,483 in 2012 expenditures because Robotx lacked clear, precise and detailed evidence of technological uncertainty and advancement.
metaDescription: Review the May 2017 Tax Court of Canada decision for Robotx Solutions Inc. regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit eligibility.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural History and Factual Context

On May 3, 2017, Justice Gaston Jorré of the Tax Court of Canada issued the judgment in Robotx Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 73 (also indexed in the official French court record as Robotx Solutions Inc. c. La Reine, 2017 CCI 73, Docket: 2016-736(IT)I). Heard under the Court's Informal Procedure, the appeal addressed a fundamental recurring conflict in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive litigation: the boundary between custom industrial engineering performed under commercial client contracts and eligible "experimental development" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Canadian Income Tax Act (the "ITA").

The appellant, Robotx Solutions Inc. ("Robotx"), is a private corporation incorporated in 2002 and headquartered in Vaudreuil-Dorion, Quebec. According to its President, Mathieu Billette, Robotx is a company that improves equipment at the request of its clients by extending its useful life, by improving its safety mechanisms in order to bring it into line with applicable standards, or by standardizing it in order to produce economies of scale. During the taxation year ending November 30, 2012, Robotx claimed SR&ED expenditures and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) in respect of engineering and automation activities carried out across specific client engagements. Following a review by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the Minister of National Revenue assessed Robotx in July 2014 and disallowed $182,483 of claimed SR&ED expenditures for the 2012 taxation year, together with the corresponding investment tax credits of $48,043, on the basis that the underlying activities did not satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED; because the appeal proceeded under the Informal Procedure, Robotx waived the portion of the denied credits exceeding $25,000, and no question of quantum was raised.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Four Disputed Contracts

At trial, two witnesses testified: Mathieu Billette, the appellant's President, who was the sole witness called by Robotx, and Jonathan Assouline, a Research and Technology Advisor with the CRA who had ruled on the eligibility of the claimed projects at the assessment stage; no expert witness was called by either party. Although the Notice of Appeal, the Reply to the Notice of Appeal and the parties at the hearing all referred to four "projects," Justice Jorré noted that this terminology (which stems from the way SR&ED claims are filed) designates only the activities for which SR&ED expenditures were claimed and not the entirety of the expenditures incurred under each contract; the issue was accordingly whether Robotx conducted SR&ED during the performance of four distinct contracts with clients during its 2012 fiscal year.

The primary engagement examined in detail by the Court was the Diageo Canada ("DICA") contract, undertaken for a producer of alcohol products at its Valleyfield plant, which had five bottling lines, each equipped with a depalletizer and a palletizer for cases of liquor bottles. The contract was for "securing the lifting platforms of depalletizers and palletizers": its stated objective was to eliminate the risk of the lifting platform falling during operations requiring an operator or mechanic to be under the machine's tray, and to bring the machines, which were obsolete and no longer supported by their original manufacturers, into line with current safety standards. Robotx obtained the contract through a call for tenders at flat-rate prices, initially intended to design a universal approach reusable on every machine, and ultimately installed a new braking device locking the platform in place together with an interlocking system that stopped everything as soon as a door giving access to the space under the platform was opened; five of the ten machines were modified before cost overruns led Diageo, with Robotx's agreement, to abandon the work on two production lines and replace them with new equipment. At approximately $81,500, the DICA project represented roughly two-thirds of the claimed SR&ED expenditures. The second engagement, by amount claimed (a little over $22,000), was the Metra Aluminum ("MEAL") contract, executed for an aluminum extrusion manufacturer and requiring Robotx to design, manufacture and install a device called a "correction roller" or "plate rectifier," integrated into an existing production line, to straighten rectangular aluminum bars coming out of the extruder without operator intervention, so that Metra could minimize handling and production costs. The third disputed engagement (about $15,000 claimed) was a contract with the municipality of Saint-Zotique ("VSZO"), awarded by municipal resolution on August 21, 2012 for a lump sum of $436,249, to upgrade and integrate the control systems of the drinking water filtration plant and 13 pumping stations, including the implementation of Ethernet telemetry in the sewage pumping stations and a new program for the filtration plant. The fourth contract, with MDA Corporation ("MDCO") and the smallest at just under $4,000, called on Robotx to design and develop new mechanisms and components, essentially a protective mechanism, to optimize the performance and safety of a CNC milling machine.

Robotx contended that the uncertainties it encountered—obsolete equipment no longer supported by its original manufacturers, the loss of operators who knew how the equipment worked, the constraints of restricted spaces, the need to combine old equipment with new-generation equipment, and the absence of information allowing the behaviour of hot, confidential aluminum alloys to be simulated—constituted technological uncertainties requiring experimental development. To substantiate its claim, the appellant relied primarily on the oral testimony of Mr. Billette alongside documentation entered as Exhibit A-1, which included the municipal tender documents and resolution (Tabs 1 and 2), order forms, purchase orders and client invoices (Tabs 4 to 9), the Form T661 project descriptions (Tab 10), a project issue sheet for the DICA project (Tab 15), two Excel files presented as records of the validation tests undertaken (Tabs 16 and 17), and photographs.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

The Minister's position was that there was no technological uncertainty in the work, that it was not carried out by means of systematic investigation or research, that only technical problems arose which could be solved by current practices forming part of existing scientific or technological knowledge, and that the appellant had not demonstrated any technological advancement. Under the Canadian federal SR&ED regime, a taxpayer seeking current expenditure deductions under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and refundable or non-refundable ITCs under subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1) and 127.1(1) (which together provide Canadian-controlled private corporations with an enhanced 35% refundable credit rate up to their expenditure limit) must first establish that the work meets the threshold definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" encompassing basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), or experimental development under paragraph (c). Because industrial automation claimants rely on paragraph (c), the work must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving "technological advancement" for creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Support work under paragraph (d)—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—is eligible only where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

In Canadian tax jurisprudence, the statutory mandate of subsection 248(1) is operationalized through the five-criterion framework established by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), 98 DTC 1839, and endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), and restated by the Federal Court of Appeal at paragraph 17 of CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, which is the formulation Justice Jorré applied:

headers: Legal Parameter under Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

cells: Criterion 1

Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Whether there existed a technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures available to competent professionals in the field.
Preamble & Paragraph (c) ("achieving technological advancement")
Criterion 2
Formulation of Hypotheses: Whether the taxpayer formulated specific scientific or technological hypotheses aimed directly at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty.
Preamble ("systematic investigation or search")
Criterion 3

Systematic Scientific Method: Whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis.
Preamble ("by means of experiment or analysis")
Criterion 4

Technological Advancement: Whether the process sought to result in a technological advancement—an increase in the stock of technological knowledge—rather than merely improving the functional utility of a commercial asset.
Paragraph (c) ("undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement")
Criterion 5
Contemporaneous Verification: Whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved was kept as the work progressed.
Evidentiary burden of proof on the balance of probabilities

body.text: The Court's Final Holding

Justice Jorré dismissed the appeal in its entirety and without costs, upholding the Minister's disallowance of the $182,483 in claimed expenditures for the 2012 taxation year. The Court concluded that Robotx had not demonstrated, with sufficiently clear, precise and detailed evidence, that the work carried out under any of the four client contracts was undertaken for the purpose of technological advancement in creating new or improving existing devices or processes, or that the uncertainties encountered were technological uncertainties rather than ordinary technical difficulties resolvable by current methods and existing knowledge; for the DICA project, the Court expressly found it unnecessary to decide whether the procedure followed accorded with the scientific method or whether the uncertainties could have been resolved by standard procedures, because the appellant had already failed to establish that the work was aimed at creating new or improved devices or processes. Furthermore, in a widely cited pronouncement at paragraph 71 of the decision, Justice Jorré clarified the evidentiary interplay between statutory requirements and contemporaneous documentation: while the ITA does not impose a rigid statutory prerequisite requiring contemporaneous documentation with specific content, discharging the legal burden of proving a systematic experimental process through clear, detailed, and precise evidence is "extremely difficult, if not impossible" without such records.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of Justice Jorré's reasons reveals four interlocking legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that defeated Robotx's SR&ED claim. These failures illustrate why custom system integrators and industrial engineering firms frequently fail to sustain SR&ED claims at the Tax Court of Canada when project governance is not explicitly decoupled from commercial delivery.
Failure to Distinguish Technological Uncertainty from Technical Complexity and Empirical Parameterization

The primary substantive flaw in Robotx's case was the conflation of commercial or operational problem-solving with "technological uncertainty" and "technological advancement". Under Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, a technological uncertainty arises only when the probability of achieving a given technical objective or the method of achieving it cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge and experience, representing a fundamental capability limit or system uncertainty in the underlying engineering domain.

In the DICA project for Diageo Canada, Robotx's objective was to secure the lifting platforms of the palletizers and depalletizers so as to eliminate the risk of the platform falling on an operator or mechanic working underneath it and to bring obsolete machines into line with current safety standards. Mr. Billette testified that the equipment was obsolete, that the original manufacturers no longer provided technical support, that operators who knew how to use the equipment were no longer available, and that a universal design had to fit within the restricted spaces imposed by the original manufacture of the machines and their position relative to the production line. Some of the information Robotx discovered during the work—for example, that one or more lifting platforms operated differently in automatic mode and in manual mode—was necessarily known to Diageo's operators but had not been communicated to Robotx, and the CRA advisor testified that such information could reasonably have been obtained from Diageo before the project was undertaken.

Justice Jorré identified the fundamental defect in claiming this activity as SR&ED: technological progress, novelty or improvement must be measured against existing scientific and technological knowledge and existing devices or processes, and where the novelty or improvement can be achieved by standard procedures, routine technical studies or current knowledge, it cannot constitute technological progress. Consequently, improving an old machine to raise its level of safety cannot represent technological progress if other machines doing the same work with the required level of safety already exist and the improvement can be made without an advance in how it is achieved; nothing in the evidence suggested that palletizers and depalletizers meeting the required safety standards were not already available, and the work was described as an upgrade to those standards. The uncertainties and problems that arose were therefore not shown to be technological: as Justice Jorré observed by analogy with the renovation of old houses, unknown situations, surprises and the effort required to solve them do not, in themselves, turn problem-solving into experimental development. Justice Jorré also adopted the observation in Les Abeilles that it is difficult to speak of technological advancement when one already knows how to obtain the result, and he would have expected any novelty or improvement sought in a process to be clearly and accurately described in relation to current processes, which was not done. Similarly, in the MEAL project for Metra Aluminum, the VSZO municipal contract and the MDCO project, the Court found no clear and detailed evidence that the uncertainties encountered could not be resolved with current methods and knowledge: new constraints imposed by the customer along the way were not, for the appellant, technological uncertainties; a reference to "3D simulation" at that level of generality (which might simply mean the use of AutoCAD software) did not demonstrate an unusual technique; and even where the contemplated device was accepted as new (MDCO), it had not been shown that unusual techniques or procedures were required.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Hypothesis Testing

Even where an industrial automation project encounters complex system integration challenges, the taxpayer must demonstrate that it followed the "total discipline of the scientific method". Satisfying this judicial standard requires a rigorous methodological sequence: the claimant must first define the baseline technological limitation and quantify why standard engineering fails, then formulate a causal hypothesis linking independent technological variables to a predicted system response, subsequently design and execute controlled experimental protocols to isolate and test those variables, and finally analyze quantitative test data to validate, modify, or refute the hypothesis.

In Robotx Solutions Inc., Mr. Billette maintained that a hypothesis was adopted by a multidisciplinary team and tested by validation, whether by 3D simulation or directly on the production line, with new hypotheses adopted until the uncertainties were dissipated, and that about a hundred tests were carried out in the DICA project; the Court, however, found that the evidence was often relatively general and vague and noted that, had it been necessary to examine the scientific-method criterion, the evidence did not seem sufficiently clear, precise and detailed to conclude that there was technological progress. Justice Jorré also cautioned that a systematic effort to resolve uncertainties and problems—like a renovation contractor who formulates a plan, revises it when problems arise, tries the new solution and revises the plan again—is not automatically an effort to overcome technological uncertainties and therefore experimental development. When a control engineer adjusts sensor positions, modifies PLC ladder logic timings, or replaces pneumatic and electrical components until a depalletizer or aluminum processing line runs smoothly without jamming, the engineer is performing iterative system tuning. Without evidence of formal hypotheses formulated prior to testing, structured test protocols, and systematic analysis of experimental data, the Court cannot distinguish the taxpayer's work from routine commissioning and debugging.
Evidentiary Collapse Due to Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation

The most enduring legal contribution of Robotx Solutions Inc. lies in Justice Jorré's analysis of the evidentiary weight of contemporaneous documentation at paragraph 71 of the judgment. In Canadian tax law, it is accepted—as Justice Jorré noted with reference to paragraph 94 of Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313—that neither the ITA nor the Income Tax Regulations require contemporaneous documentation with a specific content as a statutory condition precedent to claiming SR&ED deductions, while Justice Jorré at the same time adopted the warning of Archambault J. at paragraph 40 of 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] T.C.J. No. 478, that contemporaneous reports giving precise details of each experiment attempted should constitute the evidence of systematic investigation, and that a taxpayer who seeks to convince the Minister or the Court without such evidence is in a very precarious position. While oral testimony is legally admissible to prove that SR&ED activities occurred, reliance on those precedents often leads taxpayers into a fatal evidentiary trap when credibility and technical precision are tested at trial.

Justice Jorré reconciled this jurisprudence at paragraph 71 by drawing a sharp distinction between statutory admissibility and evidentiary sufficiency. Specifically, the Court held that although the provisions of the ITA do not require contemporaneous documentation with a specific content to demonstrate experimental development work, it remains vital for a claimant to adduce clear, detailed, and precise evidence—a task that proves extremely difficult if not impossible without contemporaneous documentation.

In Robotx, the documentary record entered as Exhibit A-1 consisted of the municipal tender documents and resolution, order forms, purchase orders and client invoices, the Form T661 project descriptions, a project issue sheet, two Excel files presented as records of the validation tests, and photographs. The order forms and invoices established the commercial scope of the work—for example, "Securing lifting platforms for depalletizers and palletizers" for Diageo—but the CRA advisor testified that the documentation identifying the tests and hypotheses presented work of a purely technical nature, namely the identification of a problem followed by its resolution through the practical application of generally available technological knowledge, and that none of the documents indicated technological limits that were sought to be exceeded, either at the start of the project or during its course. The Court further noted that the DICA work had begun in 2011, that for the MDCO project Robotx never provided the CRA with the supporting documents it claimed to hold despite being given more than five months to do so, and that for the VSZO project the evidence concerned the project as a whole rather than specific work carried out in the 2012 taxation year. Consequently, Mr. Billette's oral testimony at trial—delivered roughly four years after the end of the 2012 taxation year—remained, in the Court's words, relatively general and vague as to the functional objectives of the projects, such as securing the lifting platforms at Diageo Canada or straightening aluminum plates on the line at Metra Aluminum, rather than providing the clear, precise and detailed proof required to satisfy the judge on a balance of probabilities.
Contractual and Commercial Framing Pitfalls (Client-Ordered Equipment Enhancements)

A critical structural vulnerability highlighted by the facts of Robotx Solutions Inc. is that all four disputed claims arose directly out of commercial contracts to enhance equipment at the request of clients. In Canadian SR&ED practice, claiming SR&ED within commercial client contracts creates two distinct legal hazards that must be managed prospectively.

First, on an evidentiary and substantive level, contracts for custom equipment enhancement are governed by commercial specifications—such as throughput, reliability, safety, and operator ergonomics—rather than research objectives. In Robotx, the Court noted that the order form and invoices described the DICA work simply as "securing lifting platforms for depalletizers and palletizers," that the project issue sheet was much clearer than the Form T661 description, and that the Form T661's statement that the project aimed to improve business productivity was not borne out by the evidence; where the contemporaneous commercial record describes the scope of work in such terms without carving out distinct technological uncertainties or experimental phases, it undermines the taxpayer's later assertion on Form T661 that the contract was an experimental development project.

Second, on a statutory calculation level under subsections 37(1), 127(9), and 127(18) of the ITA, Canadian tax law strictly polices "contract payments" to prevent double-dipping and to exclude commercially funded work where the performer does not bear the financial and technical risk. Under the definition of "contract payment" in subsection 127(9), an amount paid or payable to a taxpayer by an arm's length taxable supplier (such as Diageo Canada or Metra Aluminum) for SR&ED performed for a person entitled to deduct that amount, or by a Canadian government, municipality or other Canadian public authority for SR&ED to be performed "for or on behalf of" that authority, is a contract payment and, under subsection 127(18), reduces the performer's qualified SR&ED expenditures, dollar-for-dollar, thereby reducing the ITC base. While CRA policy (reflected in Form T661 guidance distinguishing a contract for services from a contract for the sale of goods) permits a contractor to claim SR&ED if the contract is strictly for the delivery of a commercial good or general engineering asset where SR&ED is performed incidentally at the contractor's own financial risk and where the contractor retains ownership of the resulting intellectual property, failing to structure the contract terms accordingly exposes the taxpayer to complete disqualification under both subsection 248(1) as routine commercial fulfilment and subsection 127(9) as excluded contract payments (the Robotx decision itself turned solely on subsection 248(1), no contract payment or quantum issue having been raised before the Court).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Robotx Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 73, against the specific deficiencies in the taxpayer's claim and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: The Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Robotx Solutions Inc.
The Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Expectation

cells: 1. Existence of Technological Uncertainty
Subsection 248(1) ITA; Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1)

Treated the ordinary difficulties encountered in the four client contracts (DICA, MDCO, VSZO, MEAL)—obsolete equipment without manufacturer support, information held by Diageo's operators but not communicated to Robotx, customer-imposed changes, space constraints, and the integration of old and new equipment—as technological uncertainty. Framed custom client equipment enhancements as R&D without identifying why standard procedures, routine technical studies or existing knowledge were insufficient.

The taxpayer must prove objectively that a specific capability limit or system uncertainty existed in the underlying field of technology that could not be resolved through standard engineering procedures, published datasheets, or routine professional experience.
2. Formulation of Technological Hypotheses
Subsection 248(1) ITA ("systematic investigation"); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2)

Described the projects in terms of commercial and functional objectives (e.g., securing lifting platforms to meet safety standards for Diageo, straightening aluminum plates on the line for Metra, upgrading municipal control systems) and offered only a general account of hypotheses adopted by a multidisciplinary team and tested by validation; the Court found the evidence too general and vague and, for the DICA project, did not need to decide this criterion.

Clear, detailed proof of explicit hypotheses formulated ex ante that propose a specific causal relationship between technological variables and system performance to resolve the identified technological uncertainty.
3. Systematic Experimentation & Analysis
Subsection 248(1) ITA ("by means of experiment or analysis"); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3)

Relied on a general description of approximately 100 tests, 3D simulations and in-plant tests, supported by two Excel files, which the Court found did not amount to evidence sufficiently clear, precise and detailed; a reference to "3D simulation" at that level of generality did not demonstrate an unusual technique rather than ordinary AutoCAD design work.

Concrete demonstration of the scientific method in action: defined test protocols, systematic variation of parameters, collection of quantitative test data, and rigorous engineering analysis comparing experimental results against the hypothesis.
4. Purpose of Achieving Technological Advancement
Subsection 248(1)(c) ITA; Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4)

Equated functional and safety improvements to a client's commercial machinery (upgraded palletizers and depalletizers, a plate-straightening device for the aluminum line) with an advancement in technology. Justice Jorré held that improving an old machine cannot represent technological progress where other machines already do the same work with the required level of safety and the improvement can be achieved with standard procedures, routine technical studies or existing knowledge.

Proof that the work sought to generate new technological knowledge or advance the general technological baseline available to competent professionals, independent of whether the client's machine became commercially more productive.
5. Contemporaneous Evidentiary Substantiation
Robotx Solutions Inc., 2017 TCC 73 (para. 71); Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313 (para. 94); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5)

Produced tender documents, order forms, invoices, Form T661 descriptions, a project issue sheet and two Excel test files (Exhibit A-1), supplemented by oral testimony from the company's President roughly four years after the 2012 taxation year, which the Court found relatively general and vague. The documentation did not identify any technological limit sought to be exceeded, the MDCO supporting documents were never provided to the CRA, and the VSZO evidence did not isolate work performed in the 2012 taxation year.

While the ITA does not mandate a specific document format, the taxpayer must provide "clear, detailed, and precise evidence" of the experimental process. Without contemporaneous records of test protocols, data, and analysis, meeting the burden of proof via oral testimony is "extremely difficult, if not impossible".
6. Separation of SR&ED from Commercial Contract Delivery
Subsections 37(1), 127(9) ("contract payment"), and 248(1) ITA; Form T661 Part 6

Claimed portions of four commercial client contracts as SR&ED projects without the evidence establishing what proportion of each contract's expenditures was claimed, without isolating eligible experimental development from routine commercial design, installation, and commissioning, and, for VSZO, without showing which specific work in the year under appeal constituted experimental development; contract payment and IP ownership structures were not addressed.

Project accounting and contractual governance must strictly segregate commercial engineering deliverables from internal SR&ED sub-projects, proving that the claimant bore the financial risk of the R&D and did not receive "contract payments" for performing SR&ED on behalf of a Canadian payer.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Robotx Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 73, into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian industrial engineering and automation enterprises, the following two applied case studies examine realistic projects facing the exact legal pitfalls that defeated Robotx's appeal. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, commercial contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Tax Court's objections and satisfy subsections 37(1), 127(9), and 248(1) of the ITA.
Case Study 1: High-Speed Beverage Depalletizer Multi-Axis Vision and Force-Feedback Control
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment with Robotx Solutions Inc.

Automatisation Boréale Inc. ("Boréale"), a Quebec-based robotics and industrial automation integrator, is engaged by a national spirits and beverage bottler ("Distillerie Nationale") to upgrade two legacy high-speed glass bottle depalletizers on Lines 4 and 5. Distillerie Nationale is transitioning to lightweight, recycled thin-walled glass bottles stacked on warped, moisture-damaged wooden pallets with irregular cardboard slip-sheets. During high-speed sweep cycles exceeding 450 bottles per minute, the legacy depalletizers suffer from frequent bottle tip-overs and glass breakage. Skilled human operators on the plant floor can manually feather the pneumatic sweep pressure and adjust table height visually when they spot a warped slip-sheet, but the automated PLC system cannot replicate this adaptability.

If Boréale simply interviews the plant operators, adds standard laser distance sensors to measure pallet height, programs the operators' empirical "rules of thumb" into a new PLC routine, and submits the commercial invoices for the Line 4 and Line 5 upgrades as an SR&ED project, the claim will be disallowed on the same reasoning the Court applied to the DICA project in Robotx Solutions Inc., where securing Diageo's lifting platforms to meet existing safety standards was held not to be work undertaken for technological advancement. Consistent with that reasoning, the CRA and the Tax Court will treat information held by the client's operators as information that could reasonably have been obtained before the project began, and will rule that translating empirical operator knowledge into PLC code and adapting sensors to existing machinery is routine engineering achievable with standard procedures and existing knowledge, lacking technological uncertainty and contemporaneous proof of experimentation.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Decoupling SR&ED from the Commercial Upgrade

Boréale must establish a bifurcated project governance framework before engineering work commences, strictly separating the commercial equipment enhancement scope from the internal SR&ED sub-project. Under this governance structure, all routine engineering activities—including mechanical refurbishment of the Line 4 and Line 5 depalletizer frames, standard PLC cabinet wiring, safety light-curtain installation, HMI screen design, and encoding known operator sweep-speed rules for standard pallets—are assigned to commercial cost center COMM-2026-DICA and excluded entirely from Form T661. Concurrently, during preliminary engineering analysis, Boréale determines that standard 2D/3D machine vision and commercial force-torque control loops cannot calculate and compensate for the non-linear stick-slip friction coefficient of moisture-warped cardboard slip-sheets under variable glass pack harmonic vibration within the required 8-millisecond PLC scan cycle. Because standard proportional-integral-derivative (PID) damping slows the sweep cycle by 35% and fails the physical kinematics required to prevent resonant bottle oscillation, Boréale opens a dedicated internal SR&ED project (SRED-2026-01: Sub-10ms Predictive Stick-Slip Kinematic Damping Algorithm) aimed strictly at advancing real-time multi-variable control theory for non-rigid friction interfaces.
Step 2: Restructuring Commercial Contract Terms to Prevent "Contract Payment" Exclusions

To prevent the CRA from either characterizing the entire engagement as routine commercial service delivery (as the Minister successfully argued in Robotx, where the work was characterized as normal development achievable through current practices) or deducting Distillerie Nationale's payments as "contract payments" for SR&ED performed on behalf of the client under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, Boréale restructures its commercial agreement prior to execution. The Master Automation Agreement is drafted explicitly as a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of a turnkey upgraded depalletizer system meeting specified throughput metrics, rather than a time-and-materials service contract for R&D. Furthermore, Section 8 of the contract stipulates that Distillerie Nationale acquires title only to the physical hardware modifications and a non-exclusive, site-specific operational license to the compiled machine code, while all underlying mathematical models, control algorithms, source code libraries, and technological know-how developed during the engagement remain the exclusive intellectual property of Boréale for commercial deployment across its broader client base. Finally, the contract specifies that any experimental development required to achieve high-speed kinematic damping is undertaken at Boréale's sole financial risk, ensuring that warranty remediation and unbilled experimental iterations cannot be passed through to the client via change-order invoices.
Step 3: Formulating Technological Hypotheses and Tracking Systematic Experimentation

To satisfy Justice Jorré's requirement for "clear, detailed, and precise evidence" of the scientific method under paragraph 71 of Robotx, Boréale institutes a mandatory Experimentation and Hypothesis Tracking Protocol linked directly to its engineering version-control repository:

cells: EXP-01 (Months 1–2)

Hypothesis 1: Integrating high-frequency motor current ripple signatures (±0.4 A at 10 kHz) with laser triangulation of slip-sheet deflection into a Kalman filter will predict stick-slip breakaway force within ±5%, eliminating resonant bottle tipping above 450 bottles per minute.

Construct an instrumented test rig replicating Line 4 sweep kinematics. Execute 120 sweep runs across 4 controlled slip-sheet moisture levels (35%, 50%, 65% and 80% RH) while logging servo torque ripple and high-speed accelerometer data on the bottle pack.

Result: Hypothesis refuted. Servo gearbox backlash introduced a phase lag in the current ripple signal, causing destructive interference with the active damping pulse and tipping of outer-row bottles.
EXP-02 (Months 3–4)

Hypothesis 2: Decoupling the primary sweep actuator from micro-vibration damping by introducing a feed-forward acoustic emission sensor on the dead-plate coupled with a non-linear sliding-mode controller (SMC) will bypass gearbox phase lag and stabilize deceleration within 6 ms.

Modify the control architecture to implement a discrete-time sliding-mode algorithm running on a dedicated FPGA co-processor. Conduct 200 test cycles measuring dead-plate acoustic shear spikes against bottle tilt angle (θ).
Result: Hypothesis partially validated at 35–65% moisture (RH), but chattering instability occurred in the SMC boundary layer at 80% moisture due to hydroplaning friction decay.
EXP-03 (Months 5–6)

Hypothesis 3: Replacing the static SMC boundary layer with an adaptive fuzzy-logic boundary thickness modulated dynamically by initial static breakaway impulse energy will eliminate chattering across all moisture regimes while maintaining a loop execution time below 8 ms.
Program the adaptive boundary algorithm into the FPGA co-processor; run 300 validation trials across randomized mixed-moisture slip-sheets at 480 bottles per minute.

Result: Hypothesis validated. Chattering eliminated; maximum bottle tilt reduced to 2.5° with a 6.8 ms loop response, achieving a quantifiable technological advancement in high-speed non-linear friction control.

body.text: Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture for Audit and Tax Court Defence

Rather than relying on invoices, order forms, Form T661 descriptions and general test spreadsheets of the kind entered as Exhibit A-1 in Robotx—which the Court found too general and vague to establish experimental development—Boréale compiles a contemporaneous SR&ED Technical and Financial Substantiation Binder generated automatically as the work progresses. This evidentiary record commences with a dated Baseline Technology Search Memo drafted prior to EXP-01, documenting why off-the-shelf motion control blocks and published academic literature could not resolve the sub-8-millisecond non-linear stick-slip phase lag. The binder further preserves timestamped Git commit logs and code diffs corresponding strictly to EXP-01, EXP-02, and EXP-03, paired with exported CSV files of servo torque traces and accelerometer plots. Finally, engineers log their hours daily against specific experimental hypothesis codes accompanied by mandatory technical notes, cleanly separating paragraph 248(1)(c) experimental development and paragraph 248(1)(d) commensurate support work from excluded commercial installation hours.
Case Study 2: Automated Thermal-Mechanical Extrusion Control in Aluminum Processing
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment with Robotx Solutions Inc.

Systèmes Métallurgiques Avancés Inc. ("SMA"), a Canadian industrial electrical and process control engineering firm, is contracted by an aluminum extrusion manufacturer ("Profilés Aluminium") and a regional municipal water authority ("Municipalité Régionale") during the same taxation year. Under the Profilés Aluminium contract—analogous to the MEAL project in Robotx, in which Robotx designed a plate-straightening device for extruded aluminum bars—the client requests an enhancement to its aluminum billet extrusion press and quench-cooling line to reduce dimensional warping in complex thin-walled architectural profiles. Concurrently, under the Municipalité Régionale contract—analogous to the Saint-Zotique municipality project in Robotx, which involved upgrading the control systems of a drinking water filtration plant and its pumping stations—SMA upgrades pumping station variable-frequency drives (VFDs) and SCADA telemetry.

In Robotx Solutions Inc., the taxpayer claimed SR&ED expenditures under four separate commercial contracts—including the MEAL aluminum contract and the Saint-Zotique municipal contract—on the premise that the difficulties encountered in designing, integrating and commissioning custom equipment and control-system upgrades in challenging industrial environments constituted technological uncertainties. If SMA claims both contracts using general project descriptions and commercial billing records, the CRA and the Tax Court will disallow the claim in full: the municipal SCADA and VFD upgrade is textbook routine engineering (and, as with the VSZO project in Robotx, a claim that acknowledges part of the contract is not SR&ED and does not isolate the specific work performed in the year under appeal cannot succeed, while the contract is further exposed to the contract payment rules under subsections 127(9) and 127(18)), while the aluminum extrusion upgrade will fail unless SMA proves it went beyond routine closed-loop thermal control to resolve a genuine metallurgical-control system uncertainty.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Pre-Claim Eligibility Triage and Elimination of Tainted Municipal and Routine Contracts

SMA's internal SR&ED governance committee performs a rigorous Pre-Claim Eligibility Triage aligned with Northwest Hydraulic and Robotx Solutions Inc.. Reviewing the Municipalité Régionale VFD and SCADA contract, the committee notes that although the integration involved complex legacy communication protocols—such as RS-485 Modbus RTU to analog 4–20mA signal conditioning—resolving protocol incompatibilities relies on standard electrical engineering datasheets and off-the-shelf signal converters. Moreover, because payments from a municipality for work performed on its behalf constitute government assistance or contract payments under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, claiming the municipal contract would undermine SMA's credibility before the CRA and the Tax Court; consequently, the municipal contract is 100% excluded from Form T661. Turning to the Profilés Aluminium engagement, SMA strips out all commercial electrical panel fabrication, standard pyrometer installation, and safety interlock programming, isolating a single, well-defined technological uncertainty (SRED-2026-MEAL): when extruding recycled secondary aluminum alloys with fluctuating trace magnesium-silicon (Mg₂Si) precipitate concentrations, standard infrared pyrometry at the die exit suffers from spectral emissivity shifts (ε varying unpredictably between 0.05 and 0.30 due to dynamic surface oxide film growth), rendering standard closed-loop air and water-mist quench controllers unable to prevent asymmetric thermal bowing.
Step 2: Defining the Technological Advancement Objective vs. Client Equipment Enhancement

To overcome Justice Jorré's holding that enhancing client equipment does not in itself demonstrate a technological advancement, SMA defines its project objective on Form T661 Part 2 purely in terms of technological knowledge generation rather than commercial production utility. Rather than framing the project around enhancing Profilés Aluminium's extrusion quench line to eliminate profile warping and improve commercial yield—which replicates the fatal framing error in Robotx—SMA articulates its statutory objective under subsection 248(1)(c) of the ITA as determining whether real-time eddy-current impedance spectroscopy can be fused with dual-band short-wave infrared (SWIR) radiometry to compensate for dynamic surface oxidation emissivity drift on moving aluminum extrusions at 480–540 °C, thereby enabling predictive localized quench-flux modulation within 50 ms across asymmetric profile cross-sections.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring and Cost-Sharing / Risk Segregation

Because Profilés Aluminium is a taxable Canadian corporation, any payment it makes for SR&ED to be performed "for or on behalf of" Profilés Aluminium would constitute a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, reducing SMA's qualified SR&ED expenditures, and therefore its ITCs, under subsection 127(18). SMA therefore implements a two-part contractual structure to segregate commercial fulfillment from proprietary research. First, the Commercial Supply Agreement covers only the sale and installation of the physical quench-ring manifolds, standard PLC hardware, and baseline commissioning at a fixed commercial price. Second, SMA's Board of Directors formally authorizes an unbilled internal R&D budget of $165,000 for the development of its proprietary Emissivity-Compensated Eddy-Current Thermal Control Sensor Module ("EC-TCS"), and executes a Site Access and Beta Testing Addendum with Profilés Aluminium granting SMA permission to mount prototype sensor arrays on Press Line 2 during scheduled off-shift test windows at SMA's sole expense and risk, with SMA retaining 100% patent and commercial ownership of the resulting EC-TCS technology.
Step 4: Systematic Experimentation Matrix and Contemporaneous Record Protocol

To ensure that oral testimony at any future CRA review or Tax Court hearing is backed by irrefutable contemporaneous documentary proof satisfying paragraph 71 of Robotx Solutions Inc., SMA maintains a formal Experimental Test and Analysis Ledger:

headers: Experimental Setup, Test Protocol & Data Collected
Analysis of Results & Technological Advancement Achieved

cells: Phase 1: Electromagnetic-Thermal Coupling (Weeks 1–8)

Hypothesis A: High-frequency eddy-current coil impedance phase shifts (Δφ) measured post-die will correlate linearly with subsurface alloy conductivity and true bulk temperature (Tbulk), independent of surface oxide emissivity.

Fabricate water-cooled differential eddy-current probe; test across 45 extrusion billets of varying secondary alloy batches while comparing impedance phase angle against sacrificial embedded contact thermocouples.
Result: Refuted. Mechanical lift-off vibrations (±0.8 mm) of the moving extrusion profile induced parasitic inductance noise 4x larger than the thermal conductivity signal.
Phase 2: Multi-Frequency Lift-Off Cancellation (Weeks 9–18)

Hypothesis B: Exciting the probe simultaneously at two orthogonal frequencies (2 kHz skin-depth and 50 kHz surface-depth) and computing the complex impedance transfer ratio will mathematically cancel mechanical lift-off up to ±1.0 mm while isolating subsurface thermal resistivity.

Redesign signal conditioning PCB with dual-DDS synthesizers and synchronous demodulation; execute 80 controlled extrusion trials with induced mechanical vibration shims, logging raw I/Q demodulated data streams.

Result: Validated lift-off cancellation to ±0.05 mm, reducing temperature estimation error from ±25 °C to ±6 °C, but localized precipitation kinetics during rapid quenching introduced non-linear conductivity hysteresis.
Phase 3: Hybrid SWIR-Impedance State Observer (Weeks 19–30)

Hypothesis C: Coupling the dual-frequency eddy-current subsurface thermal state observer with a ratiometric SWIR pyrometer to dynamically recalibrate surface emissivity every 20 ms will eliminate precipitation hysteresis and achieve ±3 °C accuracy.

Integrate optical and electromagnetic sensor streams into an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) running on an industrial IPC; execute 110 production-scale trials measuring post-quench profile bow via laser profilometry.

Result: Hypothesis confirmed. True temperature accuracy achieved within ±2.5 °C despite oxide film variations, generating new technological knowledge in hybrid non-contact thermometry for moving non-ferrous metals.

body.text: Step 5: Evidentiary Verification Audit Trail

At year-end, SMA compiles its SR&ED claim file so that every dollar of the claimed expenditures is traceable to contemporaneous records. The technical file incorporates dated engineering notebooks and lab reports signed and timestamped weekly by the lead control engineer, containing the mathematical derivations of the dual-frequency impedance transfer function and the Extended Kalman Filter covariance matrices. On the financial accounting side, purchase orders for custom-wound ferrite cores, dual-DDS evaluation boards, and sacrificial thermocouple billets are coded directly to SRED-2026-MEAL as Form T661 materials consumed or transformed, strictly segregated from commercial electrical supplies billed to Profilés Aluminium. Finally, contemporaneous weekly timesheets are cross-referenced to specific experimental test runs (Phase 1 through Phase 3), ensuring that if the claim is audited by the CRA or litigated before the Tax Court of Canada, the taxpayer presents an unimpeachable documentary record that satisfies every legal and evidentiary standard articulated in Robotx Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 73.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court found insufficient evidence of formulated hypotheses and systematic investigation.
